analysis.one_liner: Bars the Pentagon from giving police armored vehicles, heavy weapons, grenades, silencers, and sound cannons.
analysis.headline: Backed by 49 House cosponsors from both parties, the bill never received a hearing or vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Pentagon runs a program that hands surplus military equipment — including mine-resistant armored vehicles, weapons, and aircraft — to police departments for free. This bill would have banned transfers of the most combat-style items, required police agencies to prove they can use and track what they take, and required public notice plus a government website listing every transfer. It would not have ended the program, only stripped out its most combat-oriented parts.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary residents of communities policed with military equipment. The bill's own findings state that free "military-grade" weapons and equipment "could be used inappropriately during policing efforts in which citizens and taxpayers could be harmed." Residents would gain 30-day public notice of what their local agency requests, and taxpayers would gain 100% inventory audits responding to reports of missing equipment under the program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of communities policed with military gear

how_it_helps.text: Banned future transfers to police of mine-resistant ambush-protected (MRAP) vehicles, other tactical and armored vehicles, weapons of .50 caliber or greater, grenades and grenade launchers, silencers, armored or weaponized drones, combat-configured aircraft, long range acoustic devices, and automatic weapons not suitable for law enforcement.
Removed counter-drug work as a category for which the Defense Department may transfer equipment to law enforcement.

Required receiving agencies to certify they have the personnel and training to operate the equipment, describe how they will use it, return anything surplus, and — for local agencies — notify their communities of requests through a public website and prominent postings for at least 30 days.

Required annual in-person inventories with 100 percent accountability, suspended any agency that could not account for its property, and blocked any spending on the transfer program until the Defense Secretary certified those audits to Congress.
Required the Defense Logistics Agency to run a public website listing every transfer, broken down by state, county, and recipient, and announcing each transfer 30 days before it happens.

analysis.who_pays: Local police departments, sheriffs' offices, and federal agencies that would lose free access to armored vehicles, .50-caliber weapons, grenades, silencers, and sound cannons, and would take on new certification, inventory, and reporting duties. Agencies that could not account for equipment already received would be suspended from the program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Police departments seeking free military gear

drawbacks.text: Some banned items have non-weapon uses: police agencies sought mine-resistant armored vehicles for rescues under fire and used sound cannons for long-range crowd communication, and the blanket ban would have removed them even where a department demonstrated a need.
The equipment arrives free as surplus; cutting off transfers would force departments that still want such gear to buy it with local tax dollars or go without it.
Removing the counter-drug category could limit equipment transfers tied to federal and state drug-enforcement operations.

The bill left the transfer program itself in place; it regulated what police could receive rather than ending the pipeline, and its audit duties rested on the same Defense Logistics Agency whose 2013 lifting of a weapons-transfer moratorium the bill's own findings faulted as having come 'without adequate safeguards.'

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill tackled a documented problem — a pipeline that had moved more than $4 billion in military gear to roughly 12,000 police agencies, with reports of missing equipment — using fairly modest tools: bans on the most combat-style hardware, community notice, public disclosure, and audits. The real cost falls on police departments that valued armored vehicles and certain weapons for officer protection and rescue scenarios, and on local budgets if they bought replacements. This was a middle path rather than abolition, but its transparency measures would have let taxpayers see, for the first time, exactly what their local police were receiving.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with bipartisan support in the final months of the two-year Congress, it was sent to the House Armed Services Committee and died there when no hearing or vote was ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson introduced the bill on September 16, 2014, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Armed Services.
That referral was the bill's last action of record: the committee never held a hearing or markup, and the House never voted on it.
The bill ended when the 113th Congress adjourned on January 3, 2015; House bills do not carry over to the next Congress.

It had 49 cosponsors — 45 Democrats and 4 Republicans — and the six original sponsors spanned both parties, including Georgia Democrat John Conyers alongside Idaho Republican Raul Labrador and Michigan Republican Justin Amash.

The bill responded to a program under which roughly 12,000 police organizations received nearly $500 million of surplus military equipment in fiscal 2011 alone and more than $4 billion overall, after a 2012 moratorium on weapons transfers was lifted in October 2013.
Because the bill died, the transfer program continued under its existing rules, with none of the proposed bans, community notifications, audits, or public disclosure requirements taking effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local law enforcement agencies that receive free military equipment came out ahead: the program continued unchanged, with no bans on armored vehicles and heavy weapons, no community notification, no audit requirement, and no public listing of transfers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies keeping free military gear

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Militarizing Law Enforcement Act on September 16, 2014, citing the multi-billion-dollar flow of military equipment to police and the Pentagon's lifting of its weapons-transfer moratorium.

for.name: 45 of 201 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsor John Conyers of Michigan.

for.name: 4 of 234 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Raul Labrador, Justin Amash, and Tom McClintock.

for.name: Civil liberties and community groups
for.role: National organizations such as the ACLU
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned against police militarization and for curbs on the Pentagon's surplus-equipment transfer program around the time of the bill's introduction.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 16, 2014 and took no further action of record; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Rep. Howard 'Buck' McKeon
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration before the Congress ended.

against.name: Law enforcement associations
against.what_they_did: Publicly defended law enforcement access to surplus military equipment during the post-Ferguson debate over restricting the program.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so there is no roll call, but sponsorship was bipartisan: 45 Democrats and 4 Republicans cosponsored, and the original sponsor list paired Georgia Democrats Hank Johnson and John Conyers with Republicans Raul Labrador, Justin Amash, and Tom McClintock.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: Roughly 12,000 police organizations had received over $4 billion in free military equipment, including armored vehicles and weapons; the bill would have cut off the most combat-style items and subjected recipients to audits and community notice. Their interest in keeping free, unmonitored access ran against residents' interest in less militarized policing.

industries.industry: Defense Logistics Agency (Pentagon office running the transfer program)
industries.note: The bill would have stripped the agency's discretion, requiring annual certifications, in-person inventories with 100 percent accountability, suspension of non-compliant agencies, and a public disclosure website. Its institutional interest in running the program with minimal oversight ran against the public's interest in accountability, a gap the bill illustrated by faulting the agency for lifting its 2012 weapons moratorium in 2013 without adequate safeguards.
